common_name: Lunar Eclipse Prairieblues Baptisia (Color-Changing Cream-to-Lavender False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Lunar Eclipse is a Chicago Botanic Garden Prairieblues hybrid whose buds open lemon-yellow and age through cream and pale lilac to lavender-blue, so several colors show on the spike at once.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia's deep taproot resents being moved or divided once established. Lunar Eclipse, a Prairieblues-series hybrid bred by Jim Ault at the Chicago Botanic Garden from Baptisia australis, alba, leucophaea, and sphaerocarpa, opens its buds a clear lemon-yellow and ages them through cream and pale lilac to lavender-blue as the 15-inch racemes elongate, so a single spike often displays several colors simultaneously for an unusually dynamic bloom. The dense, rounded, 3-foot clump of blue-green foliage holds its shape all season, and dark seedpods follow bloom to provide fall and winter interest while the foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Grape Escape Decadence Deluxe Baptisia (Intense Purple-Violet False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Grape Escape is a Walters Gardens Decadence Deluxe introduction bearing long spikes of dusky, intensely saturated purple-violet flowers with contrasting cream keels on a taller, fuller habit than the original Decadence series.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia's deep taproot resents being moved or divided once established. Grape Escape carries long, dense spikes of dusky, deeply saturated purple-violet, pea-like flowers accented by cream-colored keels, held well above the blue-green foliage on a fuller, taller Decadence Deluxe plant bred by Walters Gardens as a more richly colored successor to earlier purple Decadence selections. Following bloom, dark seedpods add fall and winter interest and rattle attractively in the wind, while the foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning almost like a small flowering shrub in the perennial border; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Ornamentals Trial

common_name: Cinnamon Candles Baptisia (Tall Bicolor Chocolate-and-Gold False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Cinnamon Candles is a Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights introduction (descended from B. sphaerocarpa, minor, and alba) grown for its unusually tall, bicolor chocolate-and-gold flower spikes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia's deep taproot resents being moved or divided once established. Cinnamon Candles, selected by Tony Avent at Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights Nursery from a 2007 seedling with B. sphaerocarpa, minor, and alba in its background, sends up strikingly tall flower spikes — reaching roughly 50 inches, a full 2 feet above the foliage — packed with bicolor blooms that open chocolate-brown and gold, a color combination distinct from the blues, purples, and solid yellows of most Baptisia cultivars. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest and the foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Royal Purple Prairieblues Baptisia (Deep Saturated Violet-Purple False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Royal Purple is a Chicago Botanic Garden Prairieblues hybrid with strong Baptisia australis parentage, bearing dense 18-inch spikes of deeply saturated violet-purple flowers on a vigorous, sizeable clump.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia's deep taproot resents being moved or divided once established. Royal Purple, a Prairieblues-series hybrid bred by Jim Ault at the Chicago Botanic Garden, carries dense, 18-inch spikes of deeply saturated, richly colored violet-purple, pea-like flowers in late spring; its strong Baptisia australis parentage gives it the vigor, size, and robust habit typical of that species while deepening the flower color well beyond the species' typical blue. Following bloom, dark seedpods add fall and winter interest, and the blue-green foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Plum Rosy Baptisia (Bicolor Mauve-Pink to White False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Plum Rosy is a Walters Gardens introduction whose buds open mauve-pink and lighten to near-white with age, so both colors appear together on each spike.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia's deep taproot resents being moved or divided once established. Plum Rosy bears bicolor flower spikes that open a soft mauve-pink and gradually lighten to near-white as each floret ages, so a single spike shows both colors at once, on a large, robust clump of blue-green foliage reaching 3.5 to 4 feet tall and wide. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Coker's Blazing Star (Sandhills Gayfeather)

planting.note: Sow in fall to satisfy the cold stratification the corms need, or plant nursery-propagated stock in lean, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun that mimics its native sandhill habitat.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, sharply drained, acidic soil in full sun; Coker's blazing star is a narrow endemic of the longleaf pine sandhills of the North and South Carolina coastal plain, where it grows from a corm in deep, well-drained sand alongside wiregrass and other fire-adapted species. Smooth, hairless stems carry a narrow spike of rose-purple, disc-only flower heads (lacking ray florets, like other blazing stars) in late summer and early fall, opening from the top of the spike downward and providing a valuable late-season nectar source for bumblebees, skippers, and migrating monarchs. Like other sandhill natives it depends on excellent drainage and is intolerant of heavy or consistently moist soils; it is best suited to sandy, open, fire-maintained or rock-garden-like plantings rather than a typical border.

common_name: Shinners' Gayfeather (Gulf Coast Blazing Star)

planting.note: Sow in fall to satisfy the cold stratification the corms need, or plant nursery-propagated stock in moist-to-seasonally-wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun that mimics its native longleaf pine savanna habitat.

directions: Plant in sandy, acidic, seasonally moist soil in full sun; Shinners' gayfeather is native to the longleaf pine savannas and flatwoods of Louisiana and Texas, where it grows from a globose corm in open, fire-maintained ground alongside pitcher plants and other savanna specialists. Linear, lance-shaped leaves give rise in summer to a slender spike of rose-purple, disc-only flower heads that open from the top downward, drawing bumblebees, skippers, and other pollinators through late summer. Unlike the driest-adapted blazing stars, it tolerates the seasonally moist, sandy soils typical of savanna habitat but still requires excellent drainage year-round and is intolerant of heavy clay or standing water.

common_name: Brazos Blazing Star (Aggieland Gayfeather)

planting.note: Sow in fall to satisfy the cold stratification the corms need, or plant nursery-propagated stock in well-drained clay or clay-loam soil in full sun that mimics its native post oak savanna habitat.

directions: Plant in well-drained clay or clay-loam soil in full sun; the Brazos blazing star is a narrow endemic known only from post oak savannas and open clay prairies of the Brazos Valley of central Texas, where it is considered imperiled due to habitat loss. Its branched, appressed-hairy stems distinguish it from the unbranched spikes typical of most other blazing stars, and it produces rose-purple, disc-only flower heads in late summer that open from the top of each branch downward, attracting bumblebees and other native pollinators. Because it is rare in the wild and known from only a limited range, plants offered in the trade should be nursery-propagated from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected; it is best suited to a native plant or prairie restoration planting rather than a conventional border.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: North Hills Moss Phlox (White Purple-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; North Hills establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. North Hills covers its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring with bright, starry white flowers marked by a prominent violet-purple eye at the center, a striking contrast that distinguishes it from solid-white cultivars like 'Snowflake' or 'White Delight'. Bloom is heaviest in mid-to-late spring, and plants often produce a light rebloom in fall. The tight, fast-spreading mat forms a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after the main spring bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Coral Eye Moss Phlox (Blush White Pink-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Coral Eye establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Coral Eye smothers its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring with near-white flowers washed in the faintest blush of pink and centered with a bright, contrasting pink eye, giving the mass planting a softer, more nuanced color than solid pink or solid white cultivars. The tight, fast-spreading mat knits into a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Amazing Grace Moss Phlox (Pure White Purple-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Amazing Grace establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Amazing Grace covers its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring with pure white flowers marked by only a small, delicate purple eye at the center, giving mass plantings a crisp, clean white effect that is more strongly marked than the plain white of 'Snowflake' or 'White Delight'. The tight, fast-spreading mat forms a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Drummond's Pink Moss Phlox (Dark Pink Red-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Drummond's Pink establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Drummond's Pink covers its tight, dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring with intensely saturated dark pink flowers marked with a deeper red eye, a richer and more concentrated color than the softer rose of 'Purple Beauty' or the hot pink of 'Emerald Pink'. The dense, tidy mat knits into a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Apple Blossom Moss Phlox (Pale Pink Deep-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Apple Blossom establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Apple Blossom covers its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each mid-to-late spring with soft, pale pink flowers deepening to a stronger pink at the eye, evoking the color of its namesake fruit blossom and offering a gentler pastel alternative to the more saturated pinks of 'Emerald Pink' or 'Drummond's Pink'. The mat spreads into a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Eye Candy Moss Phlox (Lavender-Pink Wine-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Eye Candy establishes quickly from container divisions set out in early spring and knits into a solid mat within a season or two.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Eye Candy, a Walters Gardens introduction, covers its refined, compact mound of dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring with light lavender-pink flowers centered by a dark, wine-purple eye, giving the mass planting more visual depth than solid-colored cultivars. Its habit is more tidy and refined than older, more vigorous selections like 'Emerald Pink', while blooming just as heavily. The dense mat forms a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and cascading over walls. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and compact, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which favors floppy growth and crown rot.

common_name: Blue Elf Woodland Phlox (Dwarf Fragrant Light Blue Wild Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Blue Elf is a diminutive seedling selection of Wild Blue Phlox forming a small, tight mat only a few inches wide, noticeably smaller in every dimension than typical woodland phlox cultivars.

directions: Plant in partial shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Blue Elf is a dwarf selection of Wild Blue Phlox (Phlox divaricata), forming a diminutive, tightly tufted mat of small green leaves only about 6 inches wide — noticeably smaller in every dimension than standard woodland phlox cultivars like 'Blue Moon' or 'London Grove Blue'. In mid-spring it sends up short, 3- to 4-inch flower spikes topped with fragrant, light blue, notch-petaled flowers, giving a proportionally large, delicate floral display relative to its diminutive size. Because of its small scale it is especially well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and the front edge of a shaded border, where larger woodland phlox cultivars would overwhelm neighboring miniature plants. Trim lightly after bloom to maintain a tidy mat, and provide consistent moisture during the growing season to prevent summer dormancy.

common_name: Sparkle White Gaura (Blush-Tinged White Compact Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sparkle White is a compact selection bred for a tidier, more floriferous habit than the sprawling wild species, blooming heavily its first year.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. Sparkle White is a compact cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri, formerly Gaura lindheimeri) bearing masses of star-shaped white flowers lightly tinged with blush pink on wiry, wand-like stems that dance in the slightest breeze. Its tidier, more compact form — roughly half the height of the straight species — keeps the airy floral display from flopping while retaining the characteristic light, naturalistic movement that gives the plant its common name. Blooming continuously from late spring into autumn with essentially no deadheading required, it is a magnet for bees and butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; cut back by one-third in midsummer if plants become open or floppy to stimulate fresh, compact growth.

common_name: So White Gaura (Sterile Pure White Compact Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; So White is a sterile, non-seeding compact selection that channels its energy into an exceptionally long, heavy bloom rather than seed production.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. So White is a compact, sterile cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri) bearing pure white, one-inch, four-petaled flowers with no pink spotting or tinting, held on wiry stems that dance in the slightest breeze. Because it produces no viable seed, the plant redirects its energy into an unusually long and heavy bloom from late spring through summer rather than into seed set, and it will not self-sow into surrounding beds the way seed-producing gaura cultivars can. Its compact, tidy habit suits smaller borders and container plantings better than the taller straight species. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; cut back by one-third in midsummer if plants become open or floppy to stimulate fresh, compact growth.

common_name: Cherry Brandy Gaura (Pink-Blushed Flowers over Bronze-Red Foliage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cherry Brandy is a compact, bushy selection notable for bronze-red-tinged foliage that contrasts with its pink, white-edged flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. Cherry Brandy is a compact, bushy cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri) distinguished by bronze-red-tinged foliage, a striking backdrop for its pink, white-edged flowers that open on wiry stems from late spring into early autumn. The foliage color deepens in cooler weather and in fuller sun, adding ornamental interest even between flushes of bloom. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; cut back by one-third in midsummer if plants become open or floppy to stimulate fresh, compact growth.

common_name: Karalee Petite Pink Gaura (Compact Red-Tinged Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Karalee Petite Pink is a diminutive Australian-bred selection well suited to containers and small borders.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. Karalee Petite Pink is a diminutive cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri), one of the shortest selections available, forming a compact clump of wiry, red-tinged stems topped with pink, four-petaled flowers that dance in the slightest breeze. Its small scale makes it especially well suited to container plantings, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny border where taller gaura cultivars would overwhelm neighboring plants. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; light shearing after flushes of bloom keeps the compact habit tidy.

common_name: Karalee White Gaura (Compact Upright White Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Karalee White is a compact, vase-shaped, free-branching selection bred for a tidier habit than the straight species.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. Karalee White is a compact, vase-shaped cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri) with a tidy, free-branching habit that carries masses of pure white, four-petaled flowers on wiry stems from late spring into autumn. Its small, upright form suits containers and the front of a sunny border better than the taller, more sprawling straight species. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; light shearing after flushes of bloom keeps the compact habit tidy and encourages continued flowering.

common_name: Pink Fountain Gaura (Dense Free-Flowering Light Pink Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pink Fountain is a dense, upright selection bred for unusually heavy, simultaneous flower production along each spike.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil — gaura demands excellent drainage and declines in consistently wet or heavy soil. Pink Fountain is a dense, upright cultivar of Lindheimer's gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri) noted for unusually floriferous spikes that hold five to eight light pink, four-petaled flowers open simultaneously — a fuller, more continuous floral display than many older gaura cultivars, whose spikes typically show only one or two open flowers at a time. The upright, well-branched habit holds up well without flopping, and the airy stems still sway attractively in the breeze. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, which also makes it resent transplanting or division; cut back by one-third in midsummer if plants become open or floppy to stimulate fresh, compact growth.
